syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

topics.title: Science as a process of discovery

concepts.learning_objective: Describe science as an ongoing process and a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity and questions.
Explain why activities, experiments and simple observations are central to learning science.
Relate human activities to the natural world and the role of science in building a sustainable world.

topics.title: Interconnected fields: materials, changes, heat and water

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise that physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences are interconnected.
Identify properties of materials and distinguish changes that can be reversed from those that cannot.
Describe how heat flows and how water moves from the seas to rain and into the ground.

topics.title: Life processes, time, light and the sky

concepts.learning_objective: State that animals and plants carry out life processes such as getting food and breathing.
Explain how early humans used the position of shadows to tell the time.
Relate day and night and eclipses to light, shadows and the movements of the Earth and the Moon.
Explain why asking interesting questions is as important as finding answers in science.
Recognise that a single answer can fit many very different questions.
Evaluate how even confirming experiments can lead to further questions and experiments.

chapters.title: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral

topics.title: Litmus as an indicator: acidic, basic and neutral substances

concepts.learning_objective: Describe litmus as a natural acid-base indicator obtained from lichens and state its colour changes.
Classify common substances as acidic, basic or neutral from their effect on blue and red litmus paper.

topics.title: Taste, touch and acids in everyday substances

concepts.learning_objective: Name the common acids present in edible substances such as lemon, tamarind, amla, curd and vinegar.
Relate the sour taste of acids and the slippery feel and bitter taste of bases, recognising the limits of taste as a test.

topics.title: Red rose and other natural indicators

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how red rose extract changes colour in acidic and basic solutions.
Identify other natural indicators such as beetroot, purple cabbage, jamun, red hibiscus and hydrangea flowers.
Use turmeric paper to detect basic substances and explain why it cannot tell acidic from neutral substances.
Explain what olfactory indicators are, using onion-soaked strips as an example.

topics.title: Neutralisation: when acids mix with bases

concepts.learning_objective: State that an acid and a base neutralise each other to form salt and water with the release of heat.
Interpret indicator colour changes that show an acidic or basic solution being neutralised.
Explain why moist baking soda relieves the sting of a red ant bite.
Choose suitable treatments for acidic, basic and neutral soils with poor plant growth.
Explain how acidic factory waste can be neutralised before it is released into water bodies.
Identify the positive and negative terminals of an electric cell and describe the cell as a portable source of electrical energy.
Explain how two or more cells must be joined to form a working battery.
Describe the filament and the two terminals of an incandescent lamp and how it produces light.
Identify the positive and negative terminals of an LED and contrast it with an incandescent lamp.

topics.title: Making a lamp glow: the electrical circuit

concepts.learning_objective: Explain that a lamp glows only when it is part of a complete path for electric current.
State the conventional direction of electric current in a circuit.
Apply the idea that current passes through an LED in one direction only.
Explain that a switch completes or breaks a circuit and can be placed anywhere in it.
Distinguish between an open circuit (switch OFF) and a closed circuit (switch ON).
Recognise and interpret the symbols for a cell, battery, lamp, LED, switch and wire.
Explain what a circuit diagram is and why standard symbols are used.
Classify materials as conductors or insulators using a conduction tester.
Explain how insulators are used to protect people from electric shocks.

chapters.title: The World of Metals and Non-metals

concepts.learning_objective: Identify metals by their metallic lustre and hardness, and recognise exceptions such as sodium, potassium and mercury.
Define malleability and give examples of metals beaten into thin sheets.
Distinguish brittle materials from malleable ones using the hammering activity.
Define ductility and relate it to the everyday uses of metal wires.
Explain sonority as the ability of metals to produce a ringing sound.
Explain that metals are good conductors of heat and relate this to cooking vessels and their handles.
Classify materials as good or poor conductors of electricity using a tester circuit.

topics.title: Effect of air and water on iron: rusting

concepts.learning_objective: Infer from Activity 4.5 that both air and water are needed for iron to rust.
Describe corrosion of metals and the methods used to prevent rusting.

topics.title: Effect of air and water on other metals

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the burning of magnesium and the basic nature of metal oxides.
Explain why a very reactive metal such as sodium is stored in kerosene.

topics.title: Substances that behave differently from metals: non-metals

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the burning of sulfur and the acidic nature of non-metal oxides.
List the properties of non-metals and use them to classify an unknown element.
Recognise that metals and non-metals are elements and that materials like plastic and wood are not.

topics.title: Uses of non-metals and metals in everyday life

concepts.learning_objective: State everyday uses of non-metals such as oxygen, carbon, nitrogen, chlorine and iodine.
Describe alloys and the special uses of metals in technology and industry.

chapters.title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

topics.title: A substance may change in appearance but remain the same

concepts.learning_objective: Identify a physical change as one in which only physical properties such as shape and size change and no new substance is formed.
Explain why changes of state such as melting and boiling of water are physical changes.

topics.title: A substance may change in appearance and not remain the same

concepts.learning_objective: Identify a chemical change as one in which one or more new substances are formed through a chemical reaction.
Use the turning of lime water milky as a test for carbon dioxide and interpret the reaction involved.
Explain why rusting of iron is a chemical change that forms iron oxide.
Describe combustion as a reaction with oxygen that gives out heat and/or light, and identify combustible substances.
Define ignition temperature and use it to explain why a substance does or does not catch fire.
State the three requirements for combustion and apply them to putting out a fire.

topics.title: Physical and chemical changes in the same process

concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish the physical and chemical changes that take place when a candle burns.
Classify everyday processes as physical, chemical, or involving both kinds of change.
Distinguish changes that can be reversed from those that cannot be reversed.
Evaluate whether a change is desirable or undesirable in a given situation, including its effect on the environment.
Explain weathering of rocks as a combination of physical and chemical changes that leads to soil formation.
Describe erosion as the movement of rock pieces, soil and sediments by wind and flowing water.

chapters.title: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change

topics.title: Growing with age: the teenage years

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the stages of human life and the age range of adolescence.
Describe the observable physical changes of adolescence, such as growth in height, voice change, acne and body hair, and recognise that their timing varies.
Define secondary sexual characteristics and classify changes seen in boys, in girls, or in both.
Explain puberty as the stage in which the body develops into an adult capable of reproduction.
Describe the menstrual cycle, its usual length, the duration of menstruation and when it stops.
Evaluate myths and taboos about menstruation using a scientific outlook.

topics.title: Emotional and behavioural changes in adolescents

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise the emotional changes of adolescence, such as mood swings, strong emotions and increased sensitivity.
Suggest positive ways to channel emotions and explain how understanding emotions helps in making better choices.

topics.title: Nutrition, personal hygiene and physical activity

concepts.learning_objective: Relate food sources to the nutrients adolescents need and to their functions in growth.
Explain good personal and menstrual hygiene practices, including proper disposal of sanitary pads.
State the benefits of regular exercise and physical activity during adolescence.

topics.title: Balanced social life and saying NO to harmful substances

concepts.learning_objective: Apply the dos and don'ts of responsible social media use and respond wisely to cyberbullying.
Explain why addictive substances are harmful and why one should say NO the first time and every time.
Explain that hormones are chemicals produced in the body that regulate growth, development, mood and behaviour.
State that hormones are produced in different parts of the body and released in response to signals from the brain.

topics.title: Conduction of heat; good and poor conductors

concepts.learning_objective: Explain conduction as heat passing from particle to neighbouring particle, from the hotter to the colder part of an object, without the particles moving.
Classify materials as good or poor conductors (insulators) of heat and relate this to their everyday uses.

topics.title: Trapped air as an insulator in clothing and houses

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how air trapped in wool, between layers of clothing or between blankets reduces heat flow because air is a poor conductor.
Explain how hollow bricks and walls of wood and mud keep houses comfortable in very hot or cold climates.

topics.title: Convection in air and in liquids

concepts.learning_objective: Explain that heated air expands, becomes lighter and rises, as seen with the paper cups, smoke and a balloon in the Sun.
Describe convection currents in heated water as hot water rising and cooler water sinking to take its place.
Compare how quickly soil and water heat up and cool down in sunlight and in shade.
Explain the formation of sea breeze by day and land breeze by night in coastal areas.

topics.title: Radiation and the three processes together

concepts.learning_objective: State that radiation transfers heat without a material medium, as from the Sun or a fire, and that all objects radiate heat.
Explain why light-coloured clothes suit summer and dark-coloured clothes suit winter.
Identify conduction, convection and radiation acting together in heating water in a pan or using a bukhari.
Describe evaporation, transpiration, condensation and precipitation as steps of the water cycle driven by the Sun's heat.
Explain how the water cycle redistributes and replenishes water while conserving its total amount on the Earth.

topics.title: Seepage of water, groundwater and its conservation

concepts.learning_objective: Relate the rate of infiltration through clay, sand and gravel to the size and connection of the spaces between particles.
Define groundwater and aquifers and explain how water is drawn from them through wells.
Explain causes of groundwater depletion and ways to conserve water such as rainwater harvesting, recharge pits and ice stupas.
Recognise that early timekeeping used natural events that repeat after definite intervals.
Describe how sundials, water clocks, hourglasses and candle clocks measured time.
Explain the working and limitations of ancient Indian water clocks, including the Ghatika-yantra.
Identify the mean and extreme positions of a pendulum and what counts as one oscillation.
Define and calculate the time period of a simple pendulum.
Analyse how the length and the bob's mass affect a pendulum's time period.

topics.title: Clocks and the SI unit of time

concepts.learning_objective: Explain that all clocks rely on a process repeating at equal intervals of time.
State the SI unit of time, convert between s, min and h, and write time units correctly.
Decide which object is faster by comparing distances covered in the same time.
Calculate speed as total distance divided by total time and state its units.
Convert speeds between m/s and km/h to compare motions.

topics.title: Relationship between speed, distance and time

concepts.learning_objective: Use the relations among speed, distance and time to find an unknown quantity.
Calculate average speed for journeys with changing speeds or stops.
Identify uniform linear motion as equal distances covered in equal intervals of time.
Recognise non-uniform linear motion in data and everyday examples.
State what a speedometer and an odometer measure in a vehicle.
Describe how teeth and tongue begin breaking down food in the mouth.
Explain how saliva breaks down starch into sugar and how the iodine test shows this.
Explain how wave-like contraction and relaxation of the food pipe walls push food to the stomach.
State the roles of the digestive juice, acid and mucus secreted in the stomach.
Describe the roles of bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice in the small intestine.
Explain how finger-like projections of the small intestine help absorb nutrients into blood.
Explain how the large intestine absorbs water and salts and forms stool.
Relate fibre, fermented foods and gut bacteria to a healthy digestive system.
Explain rumination in grass-eating animals such as cows and buffaloes.
Describe how the gizzard helps birds break down food without teeth.
Trace the path of air from the nostrils to the alveoli and state the role of each part.
Explain the movements of the ribs and diaphragm during inhalation and exhalation.
Interpret the lime water test showing that exhaled air has more carbon dioxide.
Describe the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and blood.
Distinguish breathing as a physical process from respiration as a chemical process.
State the role of the heart, blood and blood vessels in transport.
Explain how gills help aquatic animals exchange gases with water.
Relate the breathing organs of frogs and earthworms to their habitats.
Students will identify the visible changes that show a plant is growing.
Students will explain, from the three-pot activity, that plants need both sunlight and water to grow.

topics.title: Leaves: the food factories of plants

concepts.learning_objective: Students will state that plants make and store food as starch in their broad, flat, green leaves.
Students will describe the iodine test for starch in a leaf and the reason for decolourising the leaf.
Students will infer from variegated and coloured leaves that chlorophyll and sunlight are needed to make starch.

topics.title: Role of air and the products of photosynthesis

concepts.learning_objective: Students will explain, using the caustic soda experiment, that carbon dioxide from air is essential for making starch.
Students will interpret the water-plant experiment to show that oxygen is released during photosynthesis in light.
Students will write the word equation of photosynthesis and name its raw materials and products.
Students will identify stomata as tiny pores on the surface of leaves, seen in a stained leaf peel.
Students will explain how stomata allow carbon dioxide and oxygen to move in and out of leaves.
Students will explain that water and dissolved minerals move up from the roots to all parts through the xylem.
Students will explain that food made in leaves is carried to other parts through the phloem and may be stored there.
Students will describe the germinating-seed experiment and state that all parts of a plant respire.
Students will write the word equation of respiration and identify its reactants and products.
Students will analyse how photosynthesis and respiration together keep the exchange of gases balanced.
Distinguish luminous objects, which emit their own light, from non-luminous objects such as the Moon, which only reflect light.
Identify natural sources of light and artificial sources such as fire and electric lamps, including LEDs.

topics.title: Does Light Travel in a Straight Line?

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the matchbox, bent-pipe and laser activities show that light travels in a straight line.

topics.title: Light through Transparent, Translucent, and Opaque Materials

concepts.learning_objective: Classify materials as transparent, translucent or opaque by how much light passes through them.
State that a shadow forms when an object blocks light, and that a light source, an opaque object and a screen are needed to observe it.
Explain how the size and shape of a shadow change with the position of the object relative to the light source and the screen.
Describe reflection as the change in direction of light by a mirror or shiny surface.

topics.title: Images Formed in a Plane Mirror

concepts.learning_objective: State that a plane mirror image is erect, of the same size as the object and cannot be obtained on a screen.
Explain lateral inversion and its everyday uses, such as the lettering on an ambulance.
Explain how a pinhole camera forms an inverted image of an object on a screen.
Describe how plane mirrors are used in a periscope and a kaleidoscope.
Describe the Earth's rotation about its axis through the North and South Poles, from West to East, in about 24 hours.
Explain that the Sun appears to move from East to West across the sky because the Earth rotates from West to East.
Explain how the Earth's rotation causes the cycle of day and night, with half the Earth lit at any time.
Use the West-to-East rotation to explain why sunrise occurs earlier in eastern places than in western ones.

topics.title: Apparent motion of the stars and the Moon

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the Pole Star appears nearly stationary while other stars appear to move around it.
Recognise the Foucault pendulum and Aryabhata's boat analogy as ways of understanding the Earth's rotation.

topics.title: Revolution of the Earth and the changing night sky

concepts.learning_objective: Define revolution and orbit and state that the Earth revolves around the Sun in about 365 days and 6 hours.
Explain why the stars seen after sunset change gradually over a year as the Earth revolves.
Explain how the tilt of the Earth's axis and its spherical shape cause seasons, reversed in the two hemispheres.
Identify the solstices and equinoxes and the length of daytime on them in the Northern Hemisphere.
Explain how apparent size depends on actual size and distance, so the Moon can cover the Sun.
Describe the arrangement of the Sun, Moon and Earth in total and partial solar eclipses.
State safe and unsafe ways of viewing a solar eclipse.
Describe the arrangement of the Sun, Earth and Moon during a lunar eclipse.
Describe how total and partial lunar eclipses appear and that they are safe to watch.
